title: Work, jobs and the progressive
objectives: I can talk about my job, my workplace and my schedule.
I can say what is happening right now with estar plus the gerund, and form the gerund of any verb from its infinitive.
I can tell a habit (simple present) from an action in progress (progressive), and say how long something has been true with há or faz.
I can use ficar in its main meanings: stay, be located, become and ficar sabendo.
I can handle a simple phone call and a work message, and explain why words such as escritório, alô and reunião are spelled and stressed as they are.

vocabulary.note: The stress is on TÓ, the third syllable from the end (es-cri-TÓ-ri-o, with the final io counted as two syllables), and stress that far back is always marked with a written accent. The acute also shows an open o. The c is the k sound because r follows it, and the es- at the start is often said like is. The word comes from escrever, to write: a place for writing.

example.target: Meu escritório fica no centro da cidade.
example.source: My office is downtown.
example.source_literal: My office stays in-the center of-the city.

vocabulary.note: The ending ão is a nasal diphthong stressed on the last syllable by default, so the tilde only marks the nasal sound and no other accent is written: reu-ni-ÃO. The initial r is the strong h-like sound. From reunir, to bring together again. For meeting a person by chance or by appointment, encontro is used.

example.target: A reunião começa às duas da tarde.
example.source: The meeting starts at two in the afternoon.
example.source_literal: The meeting begins at-the two of-the afternoon.

vocabulary.note: Ch is the sh sound and the final unstressed e is said i: SHE-fi. The feminine is a chefe, with the same spelling, because many nouns ending in -e do not change for gender; only the article does.

example.target: O meu chefe está viajando esta semana.
example.source: My boss is traveling this week.
example.source_literal: The my boss is traveling this week.

vocabulary.note: The feminine is a colega de trabalho; the noun colega does not change, only the article. In trabalho, lh is one sound, like lli in million: tra-BA-lyu.

example.target: Ele é um colega de trabalho muito simpático.
example.source: He is a very friendly coworker.

vocabulary.note: The feminine is a cliente. The en before a consonant is a nasal vowel, the stress is on EN (second to last, the default for an ending in e), and te is said tchi: cli-EN-tchi.

example.target: O cliente está esperando na sala de reunião.
example.source: The client is waiting in the meeting room.
example.source_literal: The client is waiting in-the room of meeting.

vocabulary.note: The feminine is a funcionária. Stress on NÁ, third from the end (fun-ci-o-NÁ-ri-o), so the accent is written. The c before i is the s sound and the un is a nasal vowel. Related to função, function or duty.

example.target: A empresa tem cem funcionários.
example.source: The company has one hundred employees.

vocabulary.note: Stress on LÁ, third from the end (sa-LÁ-ri-o), so the accent is written.

example.target: O salário cai na conta no dia cinco.
example.source: The salary is paid into the account on the fifth.
example.source_literal: The salary falls in-the account on-the day five.

vocabulary.note: Used for the hours a business or employee works, as in fora do expediente, outside working hours. The x before the consonant p is said s (es-pe-di-EN-tchi), the d before i is said dj, and the en is nasal.

example.target: O expediente termina às seis horas.
example.source: Working hours end at six o'clock.
example.source_literal: The working-hours ends at-the six hours.

vocabulary.note: The feminine is a engenheira. En is nasal, the g before e is zh, nh is the sound in canyon and ei is a diphthong: en-ge-NHEI-ro.

example.target: Minha irmã é engenheira numa empresa de energia.
example.source: My sister is an engineer at an energy company.
example.source_literal: My sister is engineer in-a company of energy.

vocabulary.note: The feminine is a advogada. Brazilians slip a light i between d and v, so the word is said a-dji-vo-GA-du.

example.target: Ela é advogada e trabalha num escritório grande.
example.source: She is a lawyer and works at a large firm.
example.source_literal: She is lawyer and works in-a office big.

vocabulary.note: The same form is used for men and women: o motorista, a motorista. Nouns in -ista never change. It ends in a, so the default stress is the second to last syllable (mo-to-RIS-ta) and no accent is needed.

example.target: O motorista do ônibus foi muito simpático.
example.source: The bus driver was very friendly.

vocabulary.note: The ending -dor names the person who does the action (from vender, to sell). It ends in r, so the default is the last syllable and nothing is written: ven-de-DOR. The feminine a vendedora adds an a, which moves the default to the second to last syllable, so the stress stays on the same vowel: ven-de-DO-ra.

example.target: A vendedora me explicou tudo sobre o produto.
example.source: The salesperson explained everything about the product to me.
example.source_literal: The saleswoman me explained all about the product.

vocabulary.note: Entrevista de emprego is a job interview. En is nasal and the stress is on VIS, the second to last syllable, the default for an ending in a.

example.target: Tenho uma entrevista de emprego amanhã.
example.source: I have a job interview tomorrow.
example.source_literal: I-have an interview of job tomorrow.

vocabulary.note: From vago, empty: an opening is an empty place. It also means a parking space.

example.target: Vi uma vaga de vendedor no site da empresa.
example.source: I saw a salesperson opening on the company website.
example.source_literal: I-saw a vacancy of salesperson on-the site of-the company.

vocabulary.note: A false friend of attend: atender means to serve a customer, to see a patient or to answer the phone or the door. To attend an event is ir a or comparecer. It ends in r, so the stress is on the last syllable by default: a-ten-DER.

example.target: Pode atender o telefone, por favor?
example.source: Could you answer the phone, please?

vocabulary.note: Said mainly on the phone, to answer or to check that the other person is there; face to face use oi or olá. Borrowed from English hello and respelled. The stress is on the last syllable, which breaks the default for a word ending in o, so it takes an accent; the circumflex shows a closed o: a-LÔ.

example.target: Alô, boa tarde!
example.source: Hello, good afternoon!

vocabulary.note: The fixed phrase for asking who is on the phone uses the simple present, where English uses the progressive. Also heard: com quem eu falo? and é da parte de quem? The qu before e is the k sound with a silent u, and em is the nasal e with a weak y glide; quem is one stressed syllable and needs no accent.

example.target: Bom dia, quem fala?
example.source: Good morning, who is speaking?
example.source_literal: Good day, who speaks?

vocabulary.note: The an is a nasal vowel: trans-fe-RIR. It ends in r, so the stress is on the last syllable by default.

example.target: Vou transferir a ligação para o setor financeiro.
example.source: I will transfer the call to the finance department.
example.source_literal: I-go to-transfer the connection to the sector financial.

vocabulary.note: Um means both one and a. It is a nasal vowel, and in momento the en is nasal: mo-MEN-tu.

example.target: Um momento, por favor, já volto.
example.source: One moment, please, I will be right back.
example.source_literal: A moment, please, already I-return.

vocabulary.note: A recado is a spoken or written note passed through another person. The x after ei is the sh sound: dei-SHAR. Deixar also means to let, to allow.

example.target: Quer deixar um recado?
example.source: Would you like to leave a message?
example.source_literal: Want to-leave a message?

vocabulary.note: From ligar, to connect or tie, which is also the verb for phoning someone. The call is thought of as a connection. The ç is the s sound before a, o and u, and the ending ão is stressed by default: li-ga-ÇÃO.

example.target: A ligação caiu de novo.
example.source: The call dropped again.
example.source_literal: The connection fell of new.

vocabulary.note: Also used for a taken seat or an occupied room. The adjective agrees with its noun: a linha está ocupada, o telefone está ocupado. The c before u is the k sound.

example.target: A linha está ocupada.
example.source: The line is busy.

vocabulary.note: Feminine, like nearly all nouns in -agem (a viagem, a imagem). Men is nasal, the g before e is zh, and the ending em defaults to second to last stress, so there is no accent: men-SA-gem.

example.target: Vi a sua mensagem agora.
example.source: I just saw your message.
example.source_literal: I-saw the your message now.

vocabulary.note: In messaging, o grupo is a group chat: o grupo do trabalho, o grupo da família.

example.target: Entrei no grupo do trabalho no WhatsApp.
example.source: I joined the work group on WhatsApp.
example.source_literal: I-entered in-the group of-the work on-the WhatsApp.

vocabulary.note: In Brazil an áudio is a voice message sent in a chat. The stress is on the first syllable, third from the end (ÁU-di-o), so the accent is written; áu is a diphthong, and the d before i is said dj.

example.target: Prefiro mandar um áudio a digitar.
example.source: I prefer sending a voice message to typing.
example.source_literal: I-prefer to-send an audio to to-type.

vocabulary.note: The x between vowels has no rule and must be learned with the word; here it is ks: a-NEK-su. The stressed e is open although nothing is written, because the stress rule marks the syllable and not the quality of the vowel.

example.target: O anexo está no e-mail.
example.source: The attachment is in the email.

vocabulary.note: Marcar uma reunião, marcar uma consulta: you put the appointment on the calendar, as if marking a date. The c is k before a; before e it becomes qu to keep the k, so the imperative is marque and the preterite eu form is marquei.

example.target: Vamos marcar uma reunião para terça?
example.source: Shall we schedule a meeting for Tuesday?
example.source_literal: We-go to-mark a meeting for Tuesday?

vocabulary.note: A time limit for doing something, not a calendar date: o prazo é sexta means the time runs out on Friday.

example.target: O prazo é sexta-feira.
example.source: The deadline is Friday.

vocabulary.note: A false friend: the agenda of a meeting is a pauta. The g before e is zh and the en is nasal: a-ZHEN-da.

example.target: Minha agenda está cheia esta semana.
example.source: My calendar is full this week.

vocabulary.note: From atrás, behind: to fall behind. Atrás ends in as, whose default stress is the second to last syllable, so its last-syllable stress takes an accent. A single s between vowels is z: a-tra-ZAR. The adjective atrasado means late.

example.target: Vou atrasar uns dez minutos.
example.source: I am going to be about ten minutes late.
example.source_literal: I-go to-delay some ten minutes.

vocabulary.note: Says you learned something, usually indirectly, from someone or something else. Sabendo is the gerund of saber: the infinitive without its r, plus -ndo. The grammar note on ficar explains the construction.

example.target: Fiquei sabendo da vaga por uma amiga.
example.source: I heard about the opening from a friend.
example.source_literal: I-stayed knowing of-the opening by a friend.

grammar.title: Spelling and sound: the words of this unit
grammar.explanation:
Nothing in this unit's spelling is new. Every accent and every unusual letter below follows a rule from the first three lessons, and this note applies those rules to the new words so that you can read and write them instead of memorizing them. Two questions solve almost every word. First, where is the stress, and does it agree with the default for the word's ending? Words ending in a, e or o (with or without s) and in am, em or ens are stressed on the second to last syllable, and words with most other endings are stressed on the last syllable. When the stress disagrees with that default, a written accent marks the stressed vowel. Second, what do the neighboring letters say about how each letter is pronounced? The letters c, g, s and x, the pairs qu and gu, a vowel followed by m or n, and the pairs ch, lh and nh are all decided by their surroundings.

The largest group of accents in this unit sits on words ending in -io or -ia, such as escritório, salário, funcionário, relatório, áudio and vídeo, plus ótimo and rápido. The ending io counts as two syllables, i and o, so in escritório the stress on TÓ is the third syllable from the end: es-cri-TÓ-ri-o. No ending predicts stress that far back, so a stress there is always written. Compare vendedor, which ends in r: its default is the last syllable, the stress is there, and nothing needs to be written. The accent is always a sign that the word breaks the default of its ending. The acute accent on ó, á and é also tells you the vowel is open, and the circumflex on ô (in alô and tô) and ê (in você) tells you it is closed.

Words stressed on the last syllable break the default when they end in a, e, o or as, so they take an accent: alô (a-LÔ), já, é, está, atrás (a-TRÁS). The same holds for stressed one-syllable words in a, e or o: já, é, só, tá, tô. The last two are the everyday clipped forms of está and estou. In fast speech the es- falls away, and the stressed syllable that remains is a one-syllable word in a or o, which the one-syllable rule marks with an accent. Pôr (to put) is also one syllable, but its circumflex has a different job: it separates the verb from the preposition por (by, for). Its gerund pondo needs no accent, because the stress is on the second to last syllable and the n carries the nasal sound.

A vowel followed by m or n in the same syllable is nasal: air passes through the nose and the m or n is not a separate consonant sound. That covers cliente, entrevista, engenheiro, agenda, momento, atender, transferir, sabendo and every gerund in -ando, -endo and -indo. The endings em and ão are nasal diphthongs: mensagem and quem, reunião, ligação, apresentação and administração. In ão the stress is on the last syllable by default, so the tilde only marks the nasal sound and nothing else is written. The ç of ligação is the s sound before a, o or u. The stressed i of saindo (from sair, to leave) follows the vowel a, so the two vowels are separate syllables: sa-IN-do. Normally that stressed i takes an accent, as in saí, but when l, m, n, r or z follows the i in the same syllable the accent is not written, exactly as in ruim and sair: the consonant closes the syllable and so shows where the stress is.

The consonants follow the rules of the first lesson. The x has three values here: after ei it is sh (deixar), before a consonant it is s (expediente), and between vowels it has no rule and is learned word by word (anexo has the sound ks). The soft g is zh (agenda, mensagem, engenheiro). Ch is sh (chefe), lh is the sound in million (trabalho) and nh is the sound in canyon (engenheiro, nenhum). A single s between vowels is z (atrasar). The letter c is s before e or i (cliente, funcionário) and k before a, o, u or a consonant (marcar, ocupado, escritório). To keep the k sound before e, the spelling changes to qu, exactly as in the eu form of the preterite and in the commands: marquei, fiquei, marque, fique. The t and d before the sound i are tch and dj, and the final unstressed e is said i, so cliente is cli-EN-tchi. Brazilians also slip a light i into consonant clusters that Portuguese syllables avoid, so advogado is said a-dji-vo-GA-du. Loan words keep their original spelling and are read by Portuguese rules: e-mail is said ee-MAY-oo, with the final l as w, and alô is the English hello respelled.

Use the table as a checklist. Each row names a pattern, the words in this unit that show it and the reason for the spelling. When you meet a new word with an accent, do not ask whether to learn the accent; count the syllables, find the stress and compare it with the default.

rows: The ending io counts as two syllables, so the stress is third from the end. No ending predicts that, so an accent is always written. Acute shows an open vowel.
Stress on the third syllable from the end always takes an accent. The i of vídeo and rápido has only one sound, so the acute only marks stress.
alô, já, é, está, tá, tô, atrás
Stress on the last syllable breaks the default for endings in o, a, e and as, and a stressed one-syllable word in a, e or o is always marked. Circumflex is closed, acute is open.
The ending ão is stressed on the last syllable by default, so the tilde only marks nasality. Ç is the s sound before a, o and u. Word-initial r is the strong h-like sound.
cliente, entrevista, agenda, momento, atender, sabendo, quem, mensagem
A vowel plus m or n in the same syllable is nasal. Final e is said i and t before that i is tch. G before e is zh. The ending em is a nasal diphthong with second to last stress by default.
A stressed i after another vowel is a separate syllable and is normally marked (saí). When l, m, n, r or z follows the i in the same syllable, as the n does in saindo, no accent is written.
Pôr takes a circumflex only to separate it from the preposition por. Pondo is the irregular gerund of pôr, with no accent, since the n is nasal and the stress is second to last.
X is sh after ei, s before a consonant, and between vowels it is learned word by word (here ks).
Ch is sh, lh is the sound in million, nh is the sound in canyon, and g before e is zh.
C would be an s sound before e, so the spelling changes to qu to keep the k sound. The u is silent.
A single s between vowels is z. C before u or r is k.
Loan words keep the original spelling and are read by Portuguese rules: final l is w. Alô is the English hello respelled.

grammar.title: The present progressive: estar plus gerund
grammar.explanation:
A progressive form says that an action is in progress, unfolding at the moment you are talking about, rather than describing it as a general fact. Linguists call this a difference of aspect: the same event seen either as an ongoing process or as part of your general situation. English makes this distinction obligatory. I write is a habit and I am writing is what is happening now, and you cannot swap them. Portuguese has the same device, built in the same way: an auxiliary verb, meaning a helper verb that carries the tense and the person, plus a form of the main verb that carries the meaning. The auxiliary is estar in the present, and the main verb is in the gerund, the form that corresponds to English -ing. So Estou escrevendo is I am writing and Ela está comendo is She is eating. Only estar changes for person and number; the gerund never does.

The gerund has a single rule: take the infinitive, remove the final r and add -ndo. Falar becomes falando, comer becomes comendo and abrir becomes abrindo. The vowel of the verb family survives (a, e or i), which is why -ar verbs give -ando, -er verbs give -endo and -ir verbs give -indo. The same rule covers the verbs that look odd in the present: fazer gives fazendo, dizer gives dizendo, ler gives lendo, ver gives vendo, sair gives saindo, ir gives indo, vir gives vindo and ter gives tendo. The one everyday exception is pôr, whose gerund is pondo instead of the predicted pôndo, because pôr is a shortened form of an older poer; its relatives follow it (compor gives compondo). In pronunciation the n makes the vowel before it nasal, so falando is fa-LAN-do with no separate n sound, and the stress is on the second to last syllable, the default, so no accent is written.

Brazilian Portuguese always builds the progressive with the gerund. Estou a fazer, with estar a plus the infinitive, is the European pattern and sounds foreign in Brazil. In casual speech estou becomes tô and está becomes tá: Tô saindo agora, Tá chovendo. The negative word goes before estar: Não estou trabalhando. A question keeps the statement word order, with the question word in front: O que você está fazendo? English needs an extra helper verb for this (do you work, are you working) and Portuguese does not.

Object pronouns go directly before the verb they belong to, which here is the gerund, so in speech they sit between estar and the gerund: Estou te esperando, Ela está me ligando. Brazilians often avoid the pronoun by using the strong pronoun after the gerund: Estou esperando você. The pattern with a hyphen after the gerund (esperando-o) belongs to formal writing. Finally, the gerund is narrower than English -ing. Where English uses -ing as a noun (swimming is fun), Portuguese uses the infinitive (nadar é bom).

grammar.title: Present versus progressive
grammar.explanation:
Both tenses can be used about the present time, but they answer different questions. The simple present answers what is generally true: habits, routines, states, facts and schedules (Eu trabalho num banco, A loja abre às nove). The progressive answers what is going on during a stretch of time that includes now, with the feeling that it is temporary or unfinished (Hoje estou trabalhando em casa, Ela está estudando para a prova). The simple present is a photograph of your general situation, and the progressive is a video of the moment. English works on the same principle, so most of the time the two languages agree. The differences are at the edges, and there are a few points to watch.

First, English uses the progressive for arrangements in the future (I am leaving tomorrow). Portuguese does not: it uses the simple present with a time word, or ir plus infinitive. Viajo amanhã and Vou viajar amanhã both mean I am traveling tomorrow, and Ela liga para o senhor ainda hoje means She will call you today. You may occasionally hear a progressive for the near future in casual speech, but the present and ir plus infinitive are the pattern to copy. Second, an action in progress needs the progressive. The simple present O que você faz? asks about your job, while O que você está fazendo? asks what you are doing right now. Third, verbs of state (querer, saber, gostar, ter, ser) usually stay in the simple present even for right now, because a state is not an action unfolding: Eu quero um café, not estou querendo. Some verbs can be either, with a change in meaning: Eu moro em Curitiba is my home, Estou morando em Curitiba says the stay is temporary. The markers normalmente, sempre and todo dia point to the simple present, and agora, neste momento, hoje and esta semana often point to the progressive.

There is one more difference, which concerns how long something has been true. English says I have worked here for two years, a special present perfect, because the situation began in the past and continues. Portuguese uses the plain present, because the situation is still true: Trabalho aqui há dois anos, or Faz dois anos que trabalho aqui. The question is Há quanto tempo você trabalha aqui? Here há means it has been, and faz means it makes. The short answer Faz dois anos stands for Faz dois anos que trabalho lá. Compare the same words with the preterite, as in the lesson on the past: Faz dois anos que comecei aqui means I started here two years ago, because the starting is a finished event. The rule is that the tense follows the situation: still true now is the present, and a finished event is the preterite.

grammar.title: Ficar: stay, be located, become, ficar sabendo
grammar.explanation:
Ficar is a verb of result and duration. Its core idea is to end up somewhere or somehow and to remain there. English has no single verb for that idea, so the same Portuguese word is translated as stay, be located, get, become or keep, depending on the sentence. If you hold on to the one idea, all the uses follow. Ficar is a regular -ar verb: fico, fica, ficamos, ficam in the present, and fiquei, ficou, ficamos, ficaram in the preterite. The c becomes qu before e to keep the k sound, so the eu form of the preterite is fiquei and the command is fique.

The first use is to stay: Vou ficar em casa, Fico no escritório até as seis. The second follows from the first. Buildings, streets and cities do not move, so they stay where they are, and ficar is the everyday verb for their location: O banco fica perto do metrô. English just says is. People and movable things use estar for where they are at the moment. The third use is to become or get, with an adjective of feeling or condition: ficar nervoso, ficar cansado, ficar feliz. The adjective agrees with the subject (Ele ficou cansado, Ela ficou cansada). Ficar describes a state that comes over you and can pass; for a lasting change of role or identity, as in becoming a lawyer, Portuguese uses other verbs such as virar or tornar-se.

Four patterns are built with ficar and a small word. Ficar com means to keep or to take: Fico com este means I will take this one. Ficar de plus an infinitive means to arrange to do something, so Fiquei de ligar means I said I would call. Ficar plus a gerund means to spend time doing something: Ela ficou esperando a tarde toda means She waited around all afternoon. And ficar sabendo means to end up knowing, that is, to find out. It is ficar plus the gerund of saber, and it says that knowledge reached you, usually indirectly, through a person or a message. Because learning something is a single moment it is normally in the preterite: Fiquei sabendo da vaga por uma amiga. The preterite of saber on its own, soube, means the same thing (Soube da vaga), as in the lesson on verbs which change meaning. Ficar sabendo is more conversational and puts the news in the position of arriving to you.

grammar.title: Time expressions and phone phrases
grammar.explanation:
Ainda and já are mirror images. Ainda says a situation continues: Ainda estou trabalhando means I am still working. Já says a situation has already arrived: Já terminei means I have already finished. Their negatives are also opposites: Ainda não terminei means I have not finished yet, while Já não trabalho lá means I no longer work there. Notice the tense: Portuguese says Ainda não terminei and Já mandei o anexo with the preterite, the tense for a completed action, where English uses have plus a participle (haven't finished, have sent). In questions já means yet or ever: Você já almoçou? asks whether you have had lunch, and Você já atendeu clientes por telefone? asks whether you have ever served customers by phone.

Agora means now, and neste momento means at this moment. Neste is em plus este, in this, the contraction you met in the lessons on contractions and demonstratives, and both expressions go naturally with the progressive. Atualmente means currently, and it is a false friend of actually: atual means current, and the Portuguese for actually is na verdade. Agora há pouco means a little while ago, since há means ago in that position, and ainda hoje means later today, the same day, literally still today.

On the phone, Brazilians answer with Alô or with the name of the company. To ask who is calling, say Quem fala? (literally who speaks) or Com quem eu falo? (literally with whom I speak). In offices you will also hear É da parte de quem?, literally is it of the part of whom, meaning on whose behalf. Other phrases are Um momento, por favor; Vou transferir a ligação; A linha está ocupada; Ele não está no momento; and Quer deixar um recado? A receptionist may answer a request with Pois não, literally well no, which means certainly or how can I help you; it offers service and is not a refusal. Pode deixar, literally you can leave, means leave it to me. If the call breaks up, say A ligação caiu, literally the connection fell, or Não estou ouvindo bem. With people you do not know, use senhor and senhora, and doutor and doutora for professionals.

For messages, Brazilians write Tô chegando, Já vi, Depois eu respondo and Me avisa. Replying with an áudio, a voice message, is very common, even at work. In conversation, Nossa, short for Nossa Senhora and literally Our Lady, is an exclamation of surprise, like wow.

culture.title: WhatsApp, working hours and phone manners
culture.text:
WhatsApp is the main way Brazilians communicate, and it has moved into the workplace: companies, teams and even clients have groups, and quick decisions are made by message or by áudio. Many people do not like typing and send long voice messages instead, often with a quick Oi, tudo bem? at the start. Messages like Tô chegando (literally I am arriving) or Já vi (literally already I saw) are extremely common, and Tô chegando does not always mean the person is nearly there.

The standard working day is usually eight hours, with a lunch break known as horário de almoço (literally lunch schedule), and the official term for a regular job is emprego com carteira assinada, literally job with signed work card, meaning the employer has signed the work card and the employee gets benefits. Formal employees typically receive a 13th salary in December and thirty days of vacation a year. On the phone, people answer with Alô or the company name and use senhor and senhora with strangers. It is polite to ask É da parte de quem?, listen to the answer and then say Um momento, por favor. Professionals such as doctors and lawyers are often addressed as doutor or doutora, even when the person does not hold a doctorate; it is a mark of respect for the profession.
